stem: How does OpenAI's help-center page define prompt engineering?

choices.text: The process of designing and optimizing input prompts to effectively guide a language model's responses.
A setting under Data Controls that decides how the model interprets requests.
The training OpenAI performs on user conversations to improve the model's answers.
A certification a user completes before ChatGPT will accept complex requests.

feedback: The page defines prompt engineering as the process of designing and optimizing input prompts to effectively guide a language model's responses, and it defines a prompt as the text input that initiates a conversation or triggers a response. Choice (b) confuses the request with an account setting; Data Controls, as lesson 2 described, govern training, not interpretation. Choice (c) describes training, which is OpenAI's activity on its own models, not something the user does to a request. Choice (d) describes a requirement that appears nowhere on the page. Re-read section 01, "The vendor's definition".
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 2 (prompt engineering defined) and entry 1 (a prompt defined); guide/05/01-what-a-prompt-is.md, "The vendor's definition". No flag inherited.

stem: According to OpenAI's prompt-engineering page, what should a prompt provide so that the model understands what is being asked?

choices.text: Clarity, specificity, and enough context for the model to understand the request; ambiguity is avoided and the request is as precise as possible.
As few words as possible, because the model performs best on short prompts.
A question mark, because the model responds only to requests phrased as questions.
The name of the model that should answer, because context is set by the model choice.

feedback: The page says to ensure your prompts are clear, specific, and provide enough context for the model to understand what you are asking, and to avoid ambiguity and be as precise as possible to get accurate and relevant responses. Choice (b) contradicts the context requirement; the page asks for enough context, not for brevity. Choice (c) invents a requirement on the form of the request that the page does not state; its definition of a prompt is any text input that triggers a response. Choice (d) mistakes the model choice, which section 06 discusses as a bound on input length, for the context the page describes, which is what the request itself says. Re-read section 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 3 (clear, specific, enough context) and the sentence that follows it on the page (avoid ambiguity, be as precise as possible; GPT-03 review J1); entry 1 for distractor (c); guide/05/02-clear-specific-in-context.md, first paragraph. The section's one UNSOURCED flag (that a colleague knows what the model does not) is not what any choice turns on.

stem: A draft produced by ChatGPT reads too casually for a client letter. According to OpenAI's page and the CPA.com toolkit, which of the following is a way to get a better result?

choices.text: Name the tone in the prompt with a descriptive adjective such as formal or professional, and give the model an example of the kind of letter wanted.
Turn off "Improve the model for everyone" under Data Controls, which switches the model to a professional register.
Nothing; tone is fixed by the model and cannot be influenced from the prompt.
Upload the client's file, because the model reads the tone it should use from the client's own documents.

feedback: OpenAI's page says to use descriptive adjectives to indicate the tone, listing formal, informal, friendly, professional, humorous, and serious as words that help guide the model, and the CPA.com toolkit says that providing the model with examples helps get a better output. Choice (b) misdescribes the training switch lesson 2 covered; it governs whether conversations are used for training and has nothing to do with tone. Choice (c) is contradicted by the page's tone practice. Choice (d) invents a mechanism that neither source describes, and lesson 5 is about why a client's documents are not put into the tool without thought. Re-read section 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 5 (tone by descriptive adjectives) and file 4 entry 9 (examples help); file 8 entry 10 (the switch's label) for distractor (b); guide/05/03-tone-and-examples.md, "Tone" and "Examples". No flag inherited.

stem: The first response to a prompt is not what was wanted. What does OpenAI's prompt-engineering page say to do next?

choices.text: Review the response and refine the prompt based on the output — adjusting the wording, adding more context, or simplifying the request.
Send the same prompt again unchanged, because the model gives a different answer each time.
Start a new conversation, because a prompt cannot be refined once a response has been given.
Rate the response thumbs-down, which instructs the model to answer differently.

feedback: The page says to start with an initial prompt, review the response, and refine the prompt based on the output, and it names three ways to refine: adjust the wording, add more context, or simplify the request as needed to improve the results. Choice (b) changes nothing in the input, which is what the page says to change. Choice (c) contradicts the page's description of an iterative sequence of prompt, response, and refined prompt. Choice (d) mistakes feedback for refinement; lesson 2 described what a rating does, which is to put the conversation into training on an opted-out account, not to change the answer. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 4 (start, review, refine) and the sentence that follows it on the page (adjust wording, add context, simplify; GPT-03 review J1); file 12 entry 5 (feedback puts the conversation into training) for distractor (d); guide/05/04-refining-by-iteration.md, first paragraph and "Three moves". No flag inherited.

stem: Why does the CPA.com toolkit recommend prompting the model to return verbatim excerpts?

choices.text: Because it mimics the way a human researcher gathers information in order to reach conclusions: the model gathers the passages and the person reads them in the source.
Because the model is more accurate when it quotes than when it summarises.
Because OpenAI's terms require that responses used professionally be quoted verbatim.
Because excerpts are shorter than summaries and stay within the input maximum.

feedback: The toolkit says that by prompting the model to return verbatim excerpts you can mimic the way a human researcher gathers information in order to reach conclusions more efficiently; the point is that the person checks the source and not the summary. Choice (b) claims an accuracy effect that neither the toolkit nor any OpenAI page in this course states; an excerpt is checkable, which is a different thing from being more likely correct. Choice (c) invents a term of use. Choice (d) confuses the length of the response with the input maximum, which section 06 describes as a bound on what goes in, not on what comes out. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 7 (verbatim excerpts mimic a human researcher; the human checks the source); file 6 entry 3 and file 7 entry 3 (the input maximum) for distractor (d); guide/05/05-asking-for-verbatim-excerpts.md, "The toolkit's practice". The section's one UNSOURCED flag (that an excerpt is found in the document or not) is not what any choice turns on.

stem: According to OpenAI's pricing page, how does the input maximum for the GPT Instant model compare between the Free plan and the Business plan?

choices.text: About 12 pages of text on Free and about 40 pages on Business.
The same on every plan, because the input maximum is a property of the model.
Unlimited on every paid plan and about 12 pages on Free.
About 680 pages on Free and about 320 pages on Business.

feedback: The personal tab gives the Instant model's input maximum as about 12 pages of text on Free, and the business tab gives it as about 40 pages on Business. Choice (b) is contradicted by those two figures for the same model. Choice (c) states a figure of unlimited that appears nowhere in either grid; every plan carries a stated maximum. Choice (d) takes the Reasoning model's figures, about 680 pages on Pro and about 320 on the business plans, and assigns them to the wrong model and the wrong plans. Re-read section 06, "The Instant model".
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 7 entry 3 (Free Instant input maximum about 12 pages) and file 6 entry 3 (Business Instant input maximum about 40 pages); file 6 entry 4 and file 7 entry 4 (the Reasoning figures) for distractor (d); guide/05/06-how-much-can-go-in.md, "The Instant model". No flag inherited.

stem: Which of the following prompts follows all of the practices this lesson took from OpenAI's page and the CPA.com toolkit — clear, specific, in context, with a tone set and an example given?

choices.text: "Draft a two-paragraph cover note, in a formal tone, to accompany the attached engagement letter; the reader is a new client who has not worked with an accounting firm before. Here is a cover note we sent last year, with the client's details removed, as an example of the style."
"Write a cover note."
"Write something to go with the engagement letter, in whatever tone you think is best, about the right length."
"Draft a cover note for a new client. Be accurate."

feedback: Choice (a) is clear and specific about the task and its length, gives the context the page asks for (the reader and the purpose), names the tone with one of the page's adjectives, and supplies an example, which the toolkit says helps get a better output. Choice (b) is clear but neither specific nor in context, and sets no tone. Choice (c) is ambiguous on task, tone, and length, which is the fault the page says to remove before sending. Choice (d) adds context but leaves the tone to the model and gives no example; "be accurate" is not a practice either source describes, and lesson 4 is about why accuracy is checked afterwards rather than requested. Re-read sections 02 and 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 3 (clear, specific, enough context), entry 5 (tone by adjectives), and the sentence following entry 3 on the page (avoid ambiguity; GPT-03 review J1); file 4 entry 9 (examples); guide/05/02-clear-specific-in-context.md and guide/05/03-tone-and-examples.md. The four prompts are hypothetical illustrations that state no fact (GPT-03 review J3). No flag inherited.

stem: A CPA's first prompt asked for a summary of a long document, and the response summarised a part of it that was not the part of interest. On OpenAI's page, which description of what to do next is correct?

choices.text: Treat it as a step in an iterative sequence: review the response and refine the prompt based on the output, here by adding context that names the part of interest.
Treat the model as having failed and discard it for this task, because a model that summarises the wrong part cannot be redirected.
Switch to a plan with a larger input maximum, because a wrong summary means the document did not fit.
Ask the model which part it summarised and accept its answer, because the model can report on its own reasoning.

feedback: The page describes prompting as iterative: start with an initial prompt, review the response, and refine the prompt based on the output, by adjusting the wording, adding more context, or simplifying the request. Naming the part of interest is adding context. Choice (b) contradicts the page's description of a first prompt followed by a refined one. Choice (c) confuses a response that answered a different question with the input bound; nothing in the scenario says the document was cut, and the page's remedy is a change to the prompt. Choice (d) relies on the model to describe its own process, which nothing in this course's sources says it can do reliably, and lesson 1 said the output may be incorrect while sounding confident. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 13 entry 4 (start, review, refine) and the sentence that follows it on the page (add more context; GPT-03 review J1); file 6 entry 3 and file 7 entry 3 (the input maximum) for distractor (c); file 9 entry 2 (sounds confident even when wrong; lesson 1) for distractor (d); guide/05/04-refining-by-iteration.md, "Three moves". No flag inherited.

stem: A CPA will check whatever ChatGPT says about a document against the document itself before relying on it. On the CPA.com toolkit's account, what should the prompt ask for?

choices.text: Verbatim excerpts from the document, each with a citation to where it can be found, so that the CPA reads the passages in the source rather than the model's summary.
A summary in the model's own words, because a summary is easier to check than a quotation.
A confidence score for each statement, so that only low-confidence statements need to be checked.
The model's conclusion, stated once, so that the check has a single sentence to confirm.

feedback: The toolkit says that by prompting the model to return verbatim excerpts you can mimic the way a human researcher gathers information in order to reach conclusions, and the prompts it describes ask for a citation with each excerpt; the human checks the source, not the summary. Choice (b) reverses the practice, and a summary is the thing the excerpt is meant to replace. Choice (c) relies on expressed confidence, which OpenAI's page, as lesson 1 described, says is not a measure of reliability. Choice (d) asks the model for the conclusion the toolkit says the human should reach. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 7 (verbatim excerpts with citations; the human checks the source); file 9 entry 6 (confidence is not reliability; lesson 1) for distractor (c); guide/05/05-asking-for-verbatim-excerpts.md, "The toolkit's practice" and "Why verbatim". No flag inherited.

stem: Which statement about the amount of text that can go into one ChatGPT request is accurate on OpenAI's pricing page?

choices.text: It is bounded, and the bound differs by plan and by model: for example, about 12 pages for the Instant model on Free, about 40 on Business, and about 320 for the Reasoning model on the business plans.
It is bounded only on the Free plan; every paid plan accepts a document of any length.
It is the same for every plan and every model, because the bound is set by the document, not the service.
It is not stated anywhere on the pricing page, which gives prices and nothing else.

feedback: The page's grid gives an input maximum in pages of text for each plan and each of two models: about 12 pages for the Instant model on Free, about 40 on Business, about 320 for the Reasoning model on both business plans, and about 680 for the Reasoning model on Pro. Choice (b) is contradicted by the stated maxima on every paid plan. Choice (c) is contradicted by figures that differ across plans for one model and across models for one plan. Choice (d) has the page backwards: the captured grid gives the figures and no prices. Re-read section 06.
